universe_context:
Charlie Kirk, a 31-year-old conservative activist, media personality and close ally of President Donald Trump, was shot and killed on September 10, 2025, while speaking at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah. Kirk was the co-founder and president of Turning Point USA, a conservative youth organization active on high school and college campuses. He was appearing at the university as part of his “American Comeback Tour,” a campus speaking series built around his “Prove Me Wrong” format, in which audience members who disagreed with him were invited to debate him publicly.

The event was held outdoors on the Utah Valley University campus before a crowd estimated at about 3,000 people. Kirk was seated under a canopy and speaking into a handheld microphone when he was asked about mass shootings in the United States. A single shot was fired from a nearby rooftop and struck him in the neck. Video from the event showed spectators screaming and running as Kirk collapsed. He was taken from the scene and later died. He was survived by his wife, Erika Kirk, and their two young children.

The shooting immediately triggered a large law enforcement response and a campus shutdown. Utah Valley University canceled classes and ordered people off campus. Two people were detained in the immediate aftermath but were later released after authorities determined they were not the shooter. Investigators concluded that the gunman had fired from the roof of a campus building, then fled across the roof, dropped to the ground and escaped toward a wooded area near campus.

Federal and state officials, including the FBI, Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, Utah Department of Public Safety Commissioner Beau Mason and FBI Director Kash Patel, led a public manhunt. Authorities released surveillance images and video of a person of interest wearing a hat, sunglasses, a long-sleeve black shirt and a backpack. They also announced a $100,000 reward for information leading to an arrest. Investigators said they recovered a palm print, a shoe impression and a high-powered bolt-action rifle wrapped in a towel in a wooded area along the suspected escape route. A spent cartridge was found in the chamber and three other rounds were in the magazine. Gov. Cox said the FBI received more than 7,000 tips.

On September 12, President Trump said in a Fox News interview that a suspect had been taken into custody, saying, “I think we have him.” Authorities identified the suspect as Tyler Robinson, a 22-year-old Utah resident. Gov. Cox said a family member of Robinson contacted a family friend, who then contacted the Washington County Sheriff’s Office with information that Robinson had confessed or implied that he had committed the shooting. Cox said Robinson’s family told investigators he had become more political recently and had discussed Kirk’s upcoming appearance at Utah Valley University.

On September 16, Utah County Attorney Jeffrey Gray announced that Robinson had been charged with seven counts related to Kirk’s killing. The charges included aggravated murder, weapons-related allegations, obstruction of justice, witness tampering and committing the offense while children were present. Gray said prosecutors intended to seek the death penalty. Authorities said DNA consistent with Robinson was found on the rifle and on a towel. Prosecutors also described evidence from Robinson’s roommate and romantic partner, who cooperated with investigators. They said Robinson had left a note under a keyboard stating, “I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk and I’m going to take it,” and that investigators found a photograph of the note. Prosecutors also described text messages in which Robinson allegedly wrote, “I am, I’m sorry,” when asked if he was the person who did it, and, “I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can’t be negotiated out,” when asked why.

Kirk had been a major figure in conservative politics for more than a decade. Born on October 14, 1993, he grew up in the Chicago suburb of Prospect Heights, Illinois. He briefly attended Harper College before leaving to pursue political activism full time. In 2012, at age 18, he co-founded Turning Point USA with tea party activist William Montgomery. The organization promoted conservative ideas, including free markets and limited government, and later became closely associated with Trump-era populist conservatism. It developed a national network of student chapters and became known for campus events, conferences, viral debate clips and youth voter mobilization.

Kirk became one of the youngest speakers at the 2016 Republican National Convention and later became a frequent presence in conservative media. He launched “The Charlie Kirk Show” in 2019, building a large audience through podcasting, radio and social media. He had millions of followers on X and TikTok and was widely credited by Trump and other Republicans with helping mobilize young conservative voters, including during Trump’s 2024 campaign. His politics were strongly tied to his evangelical Christian faith, and he was known for combative views on abortion, immigration, gender, race, gun rights and the role of Christianity in public life. Supporters praised him for giving conservative students a voice on liberal-leaning campuses, while critics regarded him as divisive.

Trump announced Kirk’s death on Truth Social, writing, “The Great, and even Legendary, Charlie Kirk, is dead,” and saying that no one “understood or had the Heart of the Youth in the United States of America better than Charlie.” Trump offered condolences to Erika Kirk and the family, later ordered flags lowered to half-staff and said he would posthumously award Kirk the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor. Former President Barack Obama condemned the killing, saying such violence had no place in democracy and that he and Michelle Obama would pray for Kirk’s family. Former President Joe Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Vice President Mike Pence, actor and former California Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, Chris Pratt and Jimmy Kimmel were among others who publicly expressed condolences or denounced the shooting.

Vice President JD Vance traveled to Utah after the killing and accompanied Kirk’s family and casket back to Arizona aboard Air Force Two. Gov. Cox called the killing a political assassination and described it as an attack not only on one person but on “the American experiment.” On September 21, a public memorial service titled “Building a Legacy, Remembering Charlie Kirk” was held at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona. Tens of thousands attended, with many wearing red, white and blue. The Department of Homeland Security designated the memorial a SEAR Level 1 event, a category reserved for events of the highest national significance. Speakers included President Trump, Vice President Vance and other senior Republican and administration figures. Trump called Kirk “a martyr now for American freedom” and described him as the “greatest evangelist for American liberty.” Erika Kirk, who had been named the new CEO of Turning Point USA, addressed the crowd and said of the man charged with murdering her husband, “That young man, I forgive him.”
